Patient Vignette: Mr. A.

Mr. A. is a 79-year-old man, a retired warehouse worker, who presents with a guarded posture and a voice that rarely rises above a murmur. He was referred by his primary care physician after reporting persistent insomnia and a feeling of being “wound up too tight.” He is divorced, lives alone in a small apartment, and has minimal contact with his adult children.

The story he tells begins not in a warehouse, but in a cramped, two-room home in a village outside of Lagos. He is seven years old. He remembers the smell of kerosene and the sound of his mother’s quiet humming. The memory sharpens into a single, recurring image: his father’s belt, held by the buckle, and the way it whistled before it landed. He witnessed his father beat his mother with a terrifying, methodical regularity. He has no memory of the first time, only the feeling of it being a constant, like the weather. He learned to read the signs: the clench of his father’s jaw, the way the air in the room would go still and cold. He would freeze, a small statue in the corner, willing himself to be invisible. He never intervened, never cried out. He learned that silence was the only safety.

At 18, he left that home and that country. He came to America, found work in a warehouse, and built a life of rigid order. He married, had children, but the marriage was a quiet, brittle thing. He describes his wife as “a good woman,” but he could not tolerate the sound of her crying. He could not tolerate any loud noise. A dropped pot, a slammed door, a raised voice in an argument—these would send him into a cold sweat, his heart hammering against his ribs. He would retreat to the garage, to the basement, anywhere the sound could not reach him. His children learned not to shout. They learned to be quiet, to walk softly, to interpret his silences. The divorce came as a relief, he says, a quiet that he could finally control.

Now, at 79, the structure of the warehouse is gone. The routines that held him together—the 5 AM alarm, the heavy lifting, the predictable rhythm of the day—have vanished. He is left with the silence he craved, but it is a silence filled with noise. The memories are no longer just memories; they are visitations. He will be sitting in his chair, watching the news, and the sound of a helicopter overhead will become the whistle of a belt. He will be in the grocery store, and a child’s cry will become his mother’s muffled sobs. He flinches. He startles. He has not slept through the night in years. He wakes at 3 AM, drenched in sweat, his body rigid with a fear he cannot name.

He has a ritual. Every night, he checks the locks on his door three times. He checks the windows. He arranges his shoes by the door, precisely, so he can leave quickly if he needs to. He knows, logically, that no one is coming for him. His father has been dead for forty years. But the feeling remains—a constant, low-voltage hum of vigilance. He has begun to avoid the television news, as the images of conflict, even in distant lands, feel too close. He has stopped answering the phone. The world feels too loud, too unpredictable. He is a 79-year-old man, living in a small apartment, still trying to make himself a small, invisible statue in the corner.
